entities.name: École Normale Supérieure
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
École Normale Supérieure (ENS) is a premier higher education institution located in Paris, France, officially founded on October 30, 1794, during the tumultuous period of the French Revolution. It was established with the objective of training educators and scholars who would embody the Enlightenment ideals of reason and intellectual rigor. The school has played a pivotal role in shaping modern education in France and remains a significant institution in the realm of French intellectual and cultural life. Its influence extends beyond France, affecting educational practices and institutions across Europe and the world.

The ENS was integral in the development of modern pedagogy, fostering a rigorous academic environment that emphasized critical thinking and research. Notable figures, such as philosopher Henri Bergson and mathematician André Weil, have contributed to its legacy, producing a cadre of influential alumni who have made significant contributions to various fields, including literature, philosophy, and science. The institution has been a cradle for revolutionary ideas, where many of the French intellectual elites have been educated, thereby shaping the cultural and political discourse of the nation.

The legacy of the École Normale Supérieure is profound, as it has influenced the structure and curriculum of higher education in France and beyond. It has created a model of education that merges academic excellence with civic responsibility, inspiring institutions worldwide. The ENS has also been a breeding ground for several subsequent educational reforms and movements, including the establishment of similar 'grande écoles' in France, which further entrenched the model of elite education in the French system.
